setup: A dumbbell in each hand at your sides
Clear a stride of floor in front
execution: Step forward and land heel first
Lower the back knee toward the floor
Push off the front foot to step back
Stand tall before the next rep
faults: Don't let the front knee cave in
Don't crash down into the bottom
Don't push off the back foot to return

notes: The step forward brakes your whole body on the front leg, so it asks more of knee control than a reverse lunge. Start light and move at a steady pace.
Use a stride long enough that the front heel stays down at the bottom.
If balance goes, put the dumbbells down rather than twisting to save the rep.
Load is each dumbbell; reps are per leg.
If pain lingers or comes back, stop this exercise and get it checked by a physio or doctor.
stopIf: Pain that changes how you move

guideBrief.cameraNote: Side view at hip height, figure facing right; the near leg steps forward. Leave space in front of the figure for the stride.

keyPositions.label: Standing
keyPositions.describe: Standing tall, feet hip-width, a dumbbell hanging at each side.

keyPositions.label: Bottom
keyPositions.describe: Near foot has stepped forward about a stride, flat on the floor. Back knee just above the floor, on the ball of the back foot. Torso upright, dumbbells hanging straight down.

keyPositions.label: Push back
keyPositions.describe: Pushing off the front foot, body moving back over the back foot, front foot lifting to return beside it.

ikHints: Back foot stays planted on its forefoot through the rep
Dumbbells hang vertically from the hands
emphasise: Step lands under control, heel first
The front leg pushes the body back to standing

uncertain.note: 'Dumbbell lunge' and 'DB lunge' usually mean a forward lunge in place (StrengthLog uses that name), but some people log walking lunges under it. An import should let Ben confirm.
That a forward lunge asks more of knee control than a reverse lunge is common coaching reasoning, not a measured finding.
